shorts.title: Is the Bermuda Triangle Real? 🔍 Case #1
shorts.description:
Five Navy bombers flew out over the ocean on a training flight, and vanished off the radio. Flight 19: on 5 December 1945 five US Navy TBM Avenger bombers on a training flight from Fort Lauderdale were lost with 14 airmen after their leader became disoriented; they most likely ran out of fuel over rough seas. A PBM Mariner search plane with 13 crew was also lost, most likely in an explosion. NOAA and the US Navy say the area sees no more losses than any other busy stretch of ocean; the name comes from a 1964 Argosy story by Vincent Gaddis.

shorts.title: Lightning Never Strikes Twice? WRONG ⚡ Case #6
shorts.description:
Lightning hit the top of the Empire State Building. Then it hit it again. NOAA's National Weather Service: lightning often strikes the same place repeatedly, especially tall, pointy, isolated objects; the Empire State Building is hit an average of 23 times a year. Park ranger Roy Sullivan was struck seven times between 1942 and 1977 and survived every one.

shorts.title: The Pig War of 1859 Was REAL 🐷 Case #7
shorts.description:
A farmer pulled the trigger on a pig, and two empires started loading cannons. On San Juan Island in June 1859, American farmer Lyman Cutlar shot a Hudson's Bay Company pig that was eating his potatoes. He offered $10; the owner wanted $100. By August, 461 US soldiers with 14 cannons faced five Royal Navy warships with 70 guns and 2,140 men. Rear Admiral Robert Baynes refused to 'involve two great nations in a war over a squabble about a pig'. Nobody fired; the pig was the only casualty. In 1872 an arbitration by German Emperor Wilhelm I gave the islands to the US.

shorts.title: The US Really Built BAT BOMBS 🦇 Case #9
shorts.description:
Bats with tiny bombs strapped on flew into the rafters, and the air base caught fire. Project X-Ray: in January 1942 dentist Lytle Adams proposed strapping small timed incendiaries to Mexican free-tailed bats, and President Roosevelt approved it. On 15 May 1943 armed bats escaped and set fire to the Carlsbad Army Airfield Auxiliary Air Base in New Mexico. The program was cancelled in 1944, after about $2 million, as the atomic bomb moved ahead.
